documents.abstract: To address the problems of decontextualized vocabulary drills and the lack of adaptive, data-informed instruction, this study designs and evaluates a web-based gamified vocabulary system integrating an adaptive task sequencing algorithm, real-time learning analytics, and multimodal scenarios within a constructivist framework. In a 16-week quasi-experiment with 200 non-English-major undergraduates, the experimental group (n = 100) improved by 22.5 points in total vocabulary score, in comparison with an improvement of 11.3 points in the control group (n = 100), with the largest gains made in low-frequency word mastery (+41.5%) and vocabulary application (+39.6%). The experimental group also reported higher intrinsic motivation (4.32 vs. 3.56, p < .001), and platform logs showed task completion rising from 78.6% to 93.8% and error rate falling from 28.4% to 10.1%. Two teachers used the dashboard for data-informed instructional adjustments. These findings illustrate how web-based learning technologies can support learner autonomy and instructional decision-making in higher education.

Trustworthiness in artificial intelligence depends not only on what a model decides, but also on how it handles and explains cases in which a reliable decision cannot be made. In critical domains such as healthcare and finance, a reject option allows the model to abstain when evidence is insufficient, making it essential to explain why an instance is rejected in order to support informed human intervention. In these settings, explanations must not only be interpretable, but also faithful to the underlying model and computationally efficient enough to support real-time decision making. Abductive explanations guarantee fidelity, but their exact computation is known to be NP-hard for many classes of models, limiting their practical applicability. Computing minimum-size abductive explanations is an even more challenging problem, as it requires reasoning not only about fidelity but also about optimality. Prior work has addressed this challenge in restricted settings, including log-linear-time algorithms for computing minimum-size abductive explanations in linear models without rejection, as well as a polynomial-time method based on linear programming for computing abductive explanations, without guarantees of minimum size, for linear models with a reject option. In this work, we bridge these lines of research by computing minimum-size abductive explanations for linear models with a reject option. For accepted instances, we adapt the log-linear algorithm to efficiently compute optimal explanations. For rejected instances, we formulate a 0–1 integer linear programming problem that characterizes minimum-size abductive explanations of rejection. Although this formulation is NP-hard in theory, our experimental results show that it is consistently more efficient in practice than the linear-programming-based approach that does not guarantee minimum-size explanations.

Proactive multimodal AI can watch a user's screen, listen to speech, track interaction, and decide whether to enter unfolding work. Little is known about how people want to control what such AI may perceive and how far it may participate. Informed by a 14-person Wizard-of-Oz study, we built SpotMe, a design probe that senses screen, speech, and interaction; chooses Silence, Ask, or Assist; and lets users separately configure what it may perceive, how far it may participate, and what types of support it may provide. In a 16-person study on a civic dashboard, participants first experienced proactive help, then inspected decisions to act or remain silent, and then configured SpotMe's perception and participation. We found that participants could keep all perception channels available while lowering participation to Ask or Silence; that exposing suppressed decisions made silence interpretable and contestable; and that seeing what SpotMe used led some to change how they clicked, highlighted, and spoke. We contribute an empirical account of inspecting and controlling proactive multimodal AI by decoupling perception from participation.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) chatbots are increasingly being adopted in higher education; however, limited research has examined their pedagogical integration within learning environments. This paper reports findings from an exploratory mixed-methods case study of a GenAI chatbot embedded in a postgraduate unit at an Australian university. Designed as a pedagogically embedded learning companion, the chatbot provided contextualised guidance and functioned as a first point of contact for students seeking clarification and support. Findings indicate that students perceived the chatbot as a useful and accessible learning resource that supported engagement, reflection, and self-directed learning. Three themes emerged: first-contact pedagogical support, AI-mediated scaffolding, and human-AI complementarity. Students valued the immediacy and contextual relevance of responses while recognising the continuing importance of educator guidance. These initial findings provide insights into the design of pedagogically embedded GenAI learning companions and their potential role in supporting learning within higher education.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Developing communication skills remains a core challenge in higher education, particularly in providing scalable opportunities for practice and feedback. This study explores how artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated systems function as interactive learning environments for communication skills development. Two implementations are examined: a voice-only conversational AI-mediated system used across health disciplines and a digital human avatar used in a business unit. A mixed-methods design was employed, combining quantitative survey data and qualitative content. Findings highlighted three key affordances: repeated low-stakes practice, immediate feedback, and flexible engagement. Students reported increased confidence and perceived skill development. Limitations included conversational inaccuracies, realism, technical reliability, and feedback consistency. Importantly, findings indicate that the effectiveness of AI systems is strongly influenced by prompt design, scenario construction, and alignment with learner level. This paper reframes AI tools not as autonomous technologies, but as designed interactive learning environments requiring careful pedagogical integration. Implications are discussed for the design of AI-supported learning activities, particularly in contexts involving oral communication and authentic assessment.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Where does meaningful learning begin in an era of generative artificial intelligence (AI)? Current responses to AI in higher education have largely focused on assessment redesign, academic integrity and AI literacy. While these developments have strengthened assessment practice, they often assume that meaningful learning begins when students enter university. This paper argues that responding effectively to AI requires reconsidering this assumption. Drawing upon the learning beyond the classroom framework, it proposes assessment through transformation as a philosophy for assessment design that recognises learners’ existing educational resources and supports their development into disciplinary judgement. This paper contributes in three ways. First, it introduces the learning beyond the classroom framework as a conceptual foundation for understanding learning in AI-mediated higher education. Second, it proposes assessment through transformation as a philosophy that connects recognition, translation, transformation and disciplinary judgement within a developmental approach to assessment design. Third, it translates this philosophy into five practical principles that provide educators with a flexible lens for redesigning assessment across diverse disciplinary contexts. Rather than treating AI as the central educational challenge, the paper positions it as a catalyst for reconsidering the purposes of assessment, arguing that higher education’s enduring contribution lies in cultivating critical judgement, ethical reasoning and meaningful contribution.

In technology disciplines, students are more engaged and better prepared for employment when they experience technical work as purposeful professional practice rather than as isolated exercises (Kerven et al., 2017). Generative AI can now produce working code, configured systems and polished documentation, so students can complete tasks that mainly ask for these outputs without doing much of the work themselves. Such tasks are unlikely to hold students’ interest, and the work submitted can be weak evidence of capability. The professional judgement remains theirs: deciding what should be built, for whom, within which constraints, and with what consequences. The challenge for curriculum design is to integrate, teach and assess that judgement. This presentation describes a curriculum design we developed in response. Each unit is set in one authentic workplace context, the anchor scenario, which defines the stakeholders, constraints and outcome for the whole unit. Every session then presents a session scenario: a professional decision in that context, building on the one before. In the final assessment, students deliver the outcome the anchor scenario set. Content is taught when students need it for a decision, and assessment is set in the same context. The approach draws on situated learning, in which judgement develops through authentic activity in realistic contexts (Brown et al., 1989; Lave & Wenger, 1991), and on Action Mapping, which begins from a real workplace outcome and derives the decisions learners must make before selecting content (Moore, 2017). Narrative carries more force when scenarios accumulate rather than stand alone (Bruner, 1991). Sustained scenario structures have precedents: anchored instruction centres on one extended problem (Cognition and Technology Group at Vanderbilt, 1990), media computation organises content coverage (Guzdial, 2003), and task-driven case studies guide practice rather than judgement (Porubän et al., 2024). None spans an entire unit while structuring cumulative professional decisions, producing employer-facing artefacts, and giving AI a purposeful role. Each unit is built in three phases. The Anchor phase derives the scenario from a workplace outcome and produces a unit design plan mapping outcomes to assessments and giving every session its own scenario. The Embed phase scripts each session in full, writing assessments at the same time and checking alignment in both directions (Biggs, 1996), with every activity carrying a short connection back to the scenario. The Shift phase builds the design as web-based learning paths for delivery on campus, online or in hybrid mode. This approach now runs in more than 30 units across five discipline areas. They include a café point-of-sale system built over 11 programming sessions, a hospital network designed for a computer networking unit, and a robotic warehouse floor for an electrical engineering unit. The presentation walks through the designs themselves, alongside feedback from the teaching staff who delivered them. While the scenarios are varied, each design begins with the professional world and its people, derives the decisions from them, and lets the technology find its place inside that world.

Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly transforming higher education by reshaping how learners generate ideas, solve problems, and engage in creative knowledge construction. While existing research has primarily examined the effectiveness of AI tools on learning outcomes, writing performance, and student engagement, comparatively little attention has been paid to understanding how educators intentionally design AI-assisted creative learning experiences. This paper presents a scoping review of 49 empirical and conceptual sources on AI-assisted creativity in higher education to identify recurring instructional design practices, human–AI interaction patterns, and pedagogical strategies. Rather than focusing on technological capabilities alone, the review synthesizes how creative learning activities are structured around collaboration between learners, educators, and AI systems, while also engaging directly with mixed evidence on AI’s creative value, including findings that AI-assisted ideation can expand idea novelty under some conditions, yet produce design fixation and narrowed divergent thinking under others. Building upon this synthesis, the paper proposes a preliminary Human-Centered AI Creativity Design (HACD) framework that positions AI as a collaborative creative partner while preserving learner agency, critical reflection, and ethical decision-making. The framework offers an initial conceptual model to guide educators in designing meaningful AI-supported creative learning experiences and provides a foundation for empirical validation.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly used to support technical program managers in identifying delivery risks, but improved productivity does not necessarily imply more complete risk recognition. A critical failure mode arises when a manager initially identifies a material risk and later removes it after encountering an AI-generated assessment. This paper develops a human–AI decision-comparison method for detecting such omissions without equating disagreement with error. The framework records an unaided initial risk register, randomly assigns decision makers to a human-only second pass, ordinary AI assistance, or AI assistance with a structured challenge step, and assesses final decisions against independently adjudicated scenario risks. It distinguishes risk discovery, risk retention, and severity-weighted coverage using explicit transition measures and a multilevel comparison strategy. Domain-specific scenarios span cloud migration, data platforms, regulated delivery, and automotive system validation. The contribution is a reproducible measurement architecture for identifying whether AI assistance is associated with excess removal of risks that were previously recognized. The paper specifies testable causal contrasts and validity controls; it does not claim that an experiment has already been conducted.

This poster positions digital media (DM) assets as pedagogical decisions, arguing that their value lies not in technical sophistication, but in how effectively a medium supports learning within a given educational context (Mayer, 2020). Aligned with the ASCILITE 2026 subtheme of Human Centred Learning Design, this work introduces Digital Media as Pedagogy (DMaP), a decision-making approach that supports intentional DM selection in higher education. DMaP foregrounds pedagogical relationships and learner needs over technology guided choice, demonstrating that the suitability of different media forms varies depending on learning outcomes and the specific educational context. Meaningful media decision making requires strong collaboration between Learning Experience Designers (LEDs) and DM teams. Media design is frequently treated as a production task, downstream of the core learning content design (Thompson & Harris, 2025). This limits pedagogically aligned innovation positioning media specialists as technical implementers rather than pedagogical collaborators. Research on educational video and DM highlights that design decisions such as pacing, length, and interactivity, have a greater impact on engagement and learning than technical, even aesthetic, sophistication (Guo et al., 2014). This poster reframes the LED/DM relationship as a critical collaborative practice where expertise in pedagogy, accessibility, analytics and media production intersect. Early and ongoing collaboration supports more intentional and sustainable media design. This approach has informed changes to practice, including earlier involvement of DM specialists in subject development meetings. Positioning DM teams within early pedagogical discussions enables more cohesive alignment between learning intent and media, moving away from a more transactional style of interaction between LEDs and DM team members. The DMaP approach integrates five interconnected design lenses. The lens of pedagogical intent draws on Technological Pedagogical and Content Knowledge (TPACK) to examine whether a medium is pedagogically appropriate for specific content and learner contexts, while also legitimising collaboration across pedagogical, technological, and content expertise (Mishra & Koehler, 2006). The Cognitive Engagement lens applies the ICAP framework to examine observable learner activity, recognising that passive, active, constructive, and interactive modes each have contextual pedagogical value rather than forming a simple hierarchy (Chi & Wylie, 2014). Accessibility and Inclusion are foregrounded through Universal Design for Learning (UDL), positioning flexibility and learner choice as pedagogical strengths. This is realised through multiple means of engagement, representation and action and expressions (CAST 2024). Evidence-based Tool Selection draws on research demonstrating that digital media effectiveness varies significantly by context and design rather than novelty and considers pedagogical soundness and institutional viability (Kirkwood & Price, 2014). The final lens examines Integration and Learning Systems, recognising that, from our experience, media effectiveness appears to be influenced by LMS integration and breaks from cognitive load. DMaP questions the conventional matching of digital tool to task which tends to favour novelty over pedagogical fit. Instead, it proposes a human centred decision logic where media is selected because it aligns with intended cognitive engagement. A pedagogical approach to digital media enables accessible participation and remains feasible within institutional constraints. DMaP offers an appliable, theoretically informed approach for learning designers and DM teams.

La irrupción de la inteligencia artificial generativa en la escuela suele leerse desde dos posiciones simétricas: la adopción instrumental y la prohibición defensiva. El objetivo de este artículo es proponer un marco teórico-metodológico que supere ese dilema desde una institución educativa rural de baja conectividad en Cajibío, Cauca (Colombia). Se trata de un artículo de reflexión derivado de una tesis doctoral en curso, elaborado mediante análisis hermenéutico-conceptual de fuentes de la deconstrucción, la teoría de sistemas sociales, la crítica de la digitalidad y las epistemologías del Sur, contrastadas con antecedentes empíricos recientes sobre inteligencia artificial generativa, educación y ruralidad y traducidas en un diseño de investigación basada en diseño. Como resultado se construyen tres conceptos articulados: la superficialidad cognitiva, entendida como procesamiento del saber sin reingreso; la deconstrucción digital, operación breve y situada que irrita esa superficialidad a través de la interfaz algorítmica; y las digitalidades deconstructivas, estado plural en el que la reducción de la superficialidad se vuelve expectativa del sistema escolar. Se propone, además, la noción de acoplamiento pharmaco-deconstructivo, según la cual la decisión pedagógica no versa sobre adoptar o prohibir, sino sobre regular la dosis de irritación, y un diseño de contraste con tres condiciones, reporte estratificado y criterios de refutación declarados de antemano. Se concluye que la escasez de conectividad, leída como lugar de enunciación y no como déficit, exige pensar la mediación docente asincrónica como condición de una justicia cognitiva situada.

LLM agents increasingly drive their own learning. Self-improvement methods delegate various components of model optimization to the models themselves. As models become more capable, this motivates a basic question: do these increasingly capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve? In this paper we study an autonomous paradigm in which, given basic primitives, resources, and a general goal for self-improvement, agents construct their own self-learning algorithm for context-based optimization. Using the setting of gameplay as a testbed, a frozen LLM agent is given a compute budget and tools for collecting experience and updating text documents, and allowed to freely experiment without an externally imposed loop or access to real-world data. We find that sufficiently capable models do self-improve under these conditions, demonstrating strategies that align with classic cognitive frameworks for self-regulated learning and constructs from machine learning literature on self-generated curricula. Furthermore, we study the extent to which the learned text artifacts transfer to external benchmarks, observing improvement across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation.

Purpose: This study examines whether integrating AI personalization into a Project-Based Learning (PjBL) model produces an incremental effect on undergraduate students' critical thinking skill beyond that generated by PjBL alone, addressing the underexamined question of whether AI personalization can meaningfully intervene in critical thinking development once a pedagogically robust active-learning model is already in place. Methods: A quasi-experimental pretest–posttest control group design was employed involving 88 third-semester Business Education students at Universitas Negeri Malang, The study utilized two pre-existing classes, assigned to groups receiving either conventional PjBL (n = 46) or the PjBL learning model with AI personalization (n = 42). Data were analyzed using Wilcoxon Signed-Rank and Mann-Whitney U tests with N-Gain scoring. Findings: Both conditions improved significantly with large within-group effects (control: 70.98 to 89.91, N-Gain = 0.63, Z = −5.91, p < .001, r = 0.87; experimental: 73.14 to 89.79, N-Gain = 0.60, Z = −5.64, p < .001, r = 0.87). Neither the between-group posttest comparison (U = 886.00, Z = -0.72, p = 0.471, r = 0.08) nor the comparison of N-Gain scores (U = 840.50, Z = -1.06, p = 0.292, r = 0.11) reached significance, and the direction of both differences favored the control condition. Experiment group therefore produced no detectable advantage over control group in this setting. Research Implications: Both conditions delivered individualised, criterion-referenced formative feedback organised by the same criteria, differing only in its source, which may explain the absence of a detectable difference. The study found no evidence that AI-supported feedback was superior to peer-supported feedback under the conditions examined; these results do not establish that the two approaches are equivalent. Originality: This study examines a configuration that has received relatively little research attention: AI-based personalization integrated into established active learning models. It evaluates and compares different active learning models against one another, rather than contrasting them with passive learning. The study proposes the concept of a “pedagogical sufficiency threshold” as a testable framework for determining when AI adds substantive value to a learning model, rather than merely introducing redundancy.

Explainable AI (XAI) methods are commonly evaluated using functional correctness metrics, also called faithfulness or fidelity, which estimate how closely an explanation reflects the model’s reasoning. Higher correctness is assumed to produce better human understanding, but this link has not been tested with controlled levels. We conducted a user study ( N = 200 ) that manipulated explanation correctness at four levels (100%, 85%, 70%, 55%) in a synthetic time series classification task where participants could not rely on domain knowledge or visual intuition. Explanations were constructed to resemble feature attributions, with correctness defined against a known ground truth rather than estimated from a trained model. Participants predicted a simulated AI’s decisions from these explanations (forward simulation), and we used their forward simulation accuracy as a proxy for understanding. Correctness affected forward simulation accuracy, but not at every level: accuracy dropped at 70% and 55% relative to 100%, with no further reduction below 70% and no conclusive difference between 85% and 100%. Lower correctness reduced how many participants predicted accurately rather than lowering accuracy uniformly, and even with fully correct explanations, only a subset of participants predicted well above chance. In exploratory analyses, some participants predicted decisions accurately but described the wrong pattern when asked what the AI used, and self-reported ratings correlated with forward simulation accuracy only when explanations were fully correct. These findings suggest that, for feature-attribution-style explanations, not all differences in functional correctness translate to differences in human understanding, highlighting the need to validate functional metrics against human outcomes.

The use of generative AI (GenAI) technologies has become increasingly prevalent across Australian higher education. As these tools become an integral part of learning, they also raise concerns about over-reliance and learner agency (Resnick, 2024), authorship, ownership, and problematic forms of co-creation (Bozkurt, 2024). In Australia, 31% of the student population identify as having English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) (Australian Government Department of Education, 2024). Apart from cultural and linguistic challenges, EAL/D students also need to adapt to new academic expectations and practices that account for the impacts of GenAI technologies (Kebble, 2023). Given the unique challenges facing EAL/D student cohorts with their diverse pre-existing technological backgrounds, a gap exists in understanding how EAL/D students perceive their own work and academic contributions in relation to their use of GenAI tools. This study explores EAL/D students’ AI-assisted learning experiences and perspectives on agency through qualitative interviews conducted with 34 Master of Digital Communication students over 18 months. Findings suggest that EAL/D students are instinctively adjusting and adapting their learning practices as they engage with these technologies and making agentic decisions that support their learning. To maintain what they considered to be original and creative in their work, students developed several strategies to distinguish their own work from AI-generated output. We also found that as EAL/D students’ engagement with AI increases, they develop critical self-scrutiny. They maintain agency and ownership over their assessed work by ensuring that their (human) creativity remains central throughout the learning process. While there are some commonalities, the students in our study took diverse paths, with some students developing more nuanced and balanced approaches to using AI than others. For these students, the shift enabled them to integrate GenAI strategically while maintaining their own voice and sense of agency.

Stress management in higher education often emphasizes individual self-regulation. Less is known about how spatial configuration and ambient feedback shape mutual awareness and psychological comfort during co-located relaxation. This paper presents EchoBreset, a shared dyadic biofeedback prototype that embeds respiration sensing and ambient lighting feedback into a campus-embedded relaxation booth. We report an exploratory mixed-methods study with 108 university participants in 54 dyads, each experiencing one of three seating configurations in a semi-controlled setting. The study examined perceived relaxation, respiratory-cycle duration similarity, completion of shared progress based on both partners’ cumulative breathing contributions, and reported social interaction. Across configurations, self-report measures showed significant pre-post reductions in state anxiety and increases in relaxation ratings, while between-configuration differences in change scores were not significant. Descriptively, side-by-side seating generally showed greater respiratory-cycle duration similarity and had the highest shared-progress completion rate. It was also the most frequently mentioned preference in post-session reflections. Face-to-face seating increased partner visibility but could introduce gaze-related discomfort, whereas back-to-back seating reduced social exposure but limited access to partner cues. Participants described using partner feedback to adjust breathing, although some reported performance pressure when attempting to match a partner or track shared progress. The findings yield four design considerations: providing partner cues without requiring sustained direct gaze, clarifying the distinct roles of immediate feedback and shared progress, balancing feedback salience to support selective attention, and encouraging joint participation without imposing performance requirements. This design case contributes empirically grounded design knowledge on spatial configuration, feedback interpretation, and flexibility in attention and participation for balancing mutual awareness and psychological comfort during collaborative breathing.

Aviation operates within a highly cognitively demanding environment, where assessing pilot workload is essential for preventing errors and accidents associated with excessive or insufficient cognitive demand. This study presents a neurophysiological experiment designed to assess pilot brain activity using electroencephalography (EEG) in a high-fidelity Pilatus PC-21 flight simulator. The study focuses on the theta frequency band (4–8 Hz), given its association with mental effort and cognitive engagement. EEG signals were recorded from eight scalp locations in ten pilots during baseline conditions and three flight simulation modules with different levels of task difficulty. Subjective workload was assessed using the NASA-TLX questionnaire, completed after each simulation phase. The results showed higher theta power during the most cognitively demanding flight phase, particularly across frontal, temporal, and occipital regions. NASA-TLX results similarly indicated increased mental demand, effort, and frustration in the scenario associated with the highest cognitive workload. However, correlation analysis revealed a weak and inconsistent relationship between subjective workload ratings and EEG-derived theta measures across participants, with no clear or statistically significant overall association at the group level. These preliminary results indicate that scalp-recorded theta activity is sensitive to changes in task difficulty during flight simulation. However, given the exploratory nature of the study, the absence of flight-performance metrics, and the lack of strong correlation with subjective ratings, theta-band modulation should be interpreted as an index of task demand rather than a fully consolidated operational workload estimator.

Background: Clinical reasoning is a core competency in emergency medicine, and its structured teaching remains challenging. Generative artificial intelligence (ChatGPT) may represent a useful educational tool, but its impact on learning consolidation beyond immediate benefit remains uncertain. We assessed whether guided use of ChatGPT improves immediate documented clinical reasoning performance without compromising its retention over time. Methods: A single-center, two-arm, parallel-group, exploratory randomized controlled trial was conducted in the emergency department of Mohammed VI University Hospital, Marrakech, Morocco. Sixty medical students (5th–6th year) were randomized 1:1, using sequentially numbered, opaque, sealed envelopes generated by an independent investigator, to a ChatGPT group (simulated clinical cases with guided GPT-4o assistance) or a control group (no assistance); outcome assessors were blinded to group and time point, although participants could not be blinded to the intervention received. The primary outcome was the total Revised-IDEA (R-IDEA) score (/10), measured immediately after the intervention (T0) and again one month later under unassisted conditions (T1), analyzed by analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) adjusted for the T0 score. Results: All 60 participants were followed at T0 and T1, with no loss to follow-up. At T0, the R-IDEA score was significantly higher in the ChatGPT group (median 9.50 vs 8.50; p < 0.001; r = 0.96). At T1, the pattern reversed: the ChatGPT group showed a significant decline (median Δ = −0.75), whereas the control group improved (Δ = +1.00; p < 0.001; r = 0.96). ANCOVA confirmed a group effect at T1 favoring the control group (adjusted difference = 0.48 points, 95% CI 0.16–0.80; p = 0.004; partial η² = 0.136). Perceived confidence and benefit in the ChatGPT group were not correlated with actual performance change. Conclusions: Conclusions: Guided ChatGPT assistance improves immediate documented clinical reasoning performance, but this benefit does not persist at one month and is accompanied by poorly calibrated learner confidence. These findings support structured pedagogical oversight of generative AI in medical education, combined with active learning-consolidation strategies to ensure durable skill acquisition. Trial registration: ISRCTN registry ISRCTN13261015, registered 3 August 2026. Retrospectively registered.

documents.abstract: This study examined the effect of the working environment on employee performance in the hospitality industry in Rwanda, using Lemigo Hotel as a case study.Specifically, it assessed the effect of physical ergonomics and safety, open communication, professional growth and development, and work-life balance on employee performance.A mixed-methods descriptive research design was adopted, combining quantitative and qualitative approaches.Data were collected from a census of 198 employees using structured questionnaires, interview guides, and documentary review, and were analysed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and multiple regression in SPSS, while qualitative data were analysed thematically.The findings revealed a strong positive relationship between the combined working-environment factors and employee performance (R = 0.799), with the four predictors jointly explaining 67.4% of the variance (R² = 0.674; adjusted R² = 0.641).The regression coefficients showed that physical ergonomics and safety (B = 0.353, p = 0.025), open communication (B = 0.472, p = 0.003), professional growth and development (B = 0.676, p = 0.001), and work-life balance (B = 0.353, p = 0.009) each had a significant positive effect on employee performance, with no multicollinearity (VIF = 1.246-2.491).All four null hypotheses were rejected.The study concludes that a safe, communicative, developmental, and balanced working environment is a fundamental determinant of employee performance in the hospitality industry.It recommends that Lemigo Hotel invest in ergonomic and safety upgrades, institutionalize transparent communication channels, expand career-development pathways, and strengthen work-life balance policies to sustain and improve employee performance.

Drawing on emotion work theory and an AI-mediated communication perspective, this study uses thematic analysis to examine how emotion work is reorganized when generative AI becomes involved as a third party in communication between romantic partners. The findings indicate that some interviewees associate AI support with less concern about being judged and a lower burden of interpersonal reciprocity. They draw on its explanations and suggestions to make sense of emotions, formulate messages, and plan communication. At the same time, users need to screen and modify the generated content, and check whether the emotional attitude in it is in line with their own feelings, so as to form “authenticity work”. After the generated content is adopted, responding to the partner, fulfilling the repair arrangement, and making continuous adjustments according to the interaction between the two parties still require the input of the parties, reflecting the “limited entrustment” of emotional work. Research shows that generative AI changes the completion process of emotional work by sharing some tasks and bringing new expression management and provides an empirical basis for understanding technology-aided sincerity and relationship input.

Background As the art and design industry faces overall pressure and employment adjustments in China, how students' employment evaluations relate to their current learning behaviors requires further investigation. Grounded in Social Cognitive Career Theory, this study examined the associations among employment prospect perceptions, career self-efficacy, outcome expectations, and learning agency. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted from April to July 2026 with 591 undergraduate art and design students from four application-oriented universities in China. A two-stage partial least squares structural equation model was employed, modeling employment prospect perceptions as a formative higher-order construct comprising absolute and comparative evaluation components, while estimating its direct association with learning agency and indirect associations via career self-efficacy and outcome expectations. Bootstrap resampling was used for inference, and exploratory comparisons across academic majors were conducted using permutation tests with Bonferroni correction. Results Career self-efficacy was positively associated with learning agency (β = .598, 95% CI [.488, .696]), and the specific indirect association from employment prospect perceptions to learning agency via career self-efficacy was .263 (95% CI [.205, .323]). The direct association between employment prospect perceptions and learning agency (β = .053, p = .239) and the association between outcome expectations and learning agency (β = .100, p = .101) did not reach significance. The model explained 48.0% of the variance in learning agency. After correction, none of the 18 between-major path comparisons reached significance. Conclusions Career self-efficacy serves as an important linking factor connecting employment prospect perceptions with learning agency. The study provides evidence for applying SCCT in career preparatory learning contexts and suggests that career support may integrate employment information with professional competence experiences. The temporal order and causal direction of these associations require longitudinal research for validation.

Purpose This study aims to examine how employee empowerment and task delegation influence workplace creativity through harmonious and obsessive work passion, and whether organizational vision awareness (OVA) strengthens these motivational pathways in a public sector context. Design/methodology/approach Survey data were collected from 533 employees across two Namibian public sector ministries using stratified random sampling. Employee self-reports were matched with supervisor ratings of incremental and radical creativity to reduce common method bias. Structural equation modeling tested indirect and conditional relationships among empowerment, delegation, work passion and creativity. Findings Empowerment and task delegation are indirectly related to creativity through distinct forms of work passion. Harmonious passion predicts both incremental and radical creativity, whereas obsessive passion is primarily linked to incremental creativity. OVA strengthens selected motivational pathways, showing that shared vision enhances the effectiveness of leadership practices in fostering creativity. Originality/value This study demonstrates that empowerment and delegation operate through differentiated passion-based mechanisms rather than uniform effects. By distinguishing between incremental and radical creativity, it clarifies how motivational processes translate managerial practices into distinct creative outcomes. It further extends the literature by identifying OVA as a boundary condition and by providing evidence from an underexplored African public sector context.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming clinical practice, and digital-health and assessment frameworks increasingly identify capabilities that involve using AI. Translating these expectations into a crowded, vertically integrated medical curriculum is a substantial implementation challenge. This case study describes how one Australian graduate medical program has approached integrating AI literacy education, teaching with AI and assessment reform. A cross-functional working group, convened by the Dean of Medicine and chaired by the first author, comprising academic, clinical, professional, library and student members and reporting to the School Executive, has coordinated the program’s early response through monthly meetings, program planning day sessions and engagement with grassroots pilots, including a trial of an AI-powered communication skills simulation platform. We describe the challenges encountered: defining AI literacy content without a settled national curriculum, negotiating curriculum space across all year levels, sustaining communication among diverse stakeholders, developing staff capability across attitudes ranging from enthusiasm to sustained concern, responding to student concerns about AI-enabled learning tools, and redesigning assessment to comply with institution-wide reform while preserving a programmatic assessment system. We share practical lessons for other programs, arguing that an enabling, relationship-centred approach may help coordinate change.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This study examined how Biology teachers engage students through Project-Based Learning (PBL) in six-day lower secondary schools in Gasabo District, Rwanda, guided by three objectives: teachers' understanding of PBL, their design and implementation of PBL activities, and PBL's contribution to students' motivation.A convergent parallel mixed-methods design was adopted within the pragmatic paradigm, with all 30 Biology teachers in the six schools included through census sampling.Data were collected using a questionnaire, a semi-structured interview guide, and a classroom observation checklist, and triangulated across the three sources; quantitative data were analyzed in SPSS Version 26 using descriptive statistics and multiple regression, while qualitative data were analyzed thematically.Teachers showed a strong theoretical understanding of PBL (M = 4.00-4.13)but a comparatively weaker command of implementation and assessment procedures (M = 3.70-3.73),a gap attributed to limited time, large classes, and insufficient materials rather than to any deficit in conceptual knowledge.Effective PBL activities were curriculum-aligned, collaborative, inquiry-based, and teacher-facilitated.Authentic, real-life projects emerged as the strongest predictor of behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement, with the largest effect on cognitive engagement (β = 0.451, p = .001).PBL is an effective, learner-centred approach for engaging Biology students, and its full potential is currently constrained more by institutional and resource conditions than by teachers' understanding of, or commitment to, the approach.Strengthening teacher capacity in PBL implementation and assessment, and providing adequate instructional time and materials, is recommended.

Generative AI is changing how students complete assessments and demonstrate what they know. As AI tools become part of everyday study, final assessment submissions alone may not provide sufficient evidence of how students think, solve problems, or develop understanding throughout the learning process. This paper introduces Engineering Visible Thinking (EVT), a human-centred assessment framework designed for the AI era. Rather than focusing on whether students use AI, EVT focuses on designing assessments that generate multiple forms of evidence to support judgements about student learning. The framework is built around three connected elements: visible thinking, process evidence, and capability validation. The paper draws on the design of a new Applied IT degree and includes a detailed example from the first-year Networking Fundamentals course to illustrate the application of the EVT framework in practice. The paper argues that the real challenge is not detecting AI use but designing assessments that provide evidence to support judgements about students’ learning and capability. By extending assessment beyond final products to include evidence of thinking, process and demonstrated competence, EVT offers a practical approach to assessment design that keeps people, not technology, at the centre of learning.

Universities’ education-related artificial intelligence (AI) principles are vital statements that accessibly outline the institutions’ stances towards the technology’s use in learning. Ensuring the cultural sensitivity of these principles is vital given today’s superdiversity in higher education. This paper presents insights from research examining the cultural sensitivity of these principles, using Australian universities as its case study. The research covers 42 Australian universities, with AI principle content from 28 universities analysed using a qualitative content analysis. The findings show that the idea of cultural sensitivity is generally addressed at a surface level. The paper argues that all universities not only need to provide robust, publicly accessible educational AI principles, but also actively integrate cultural sensitivity into these principles. Based on the paper’s research insights, a novel framework is provided to support this integration.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The deployment of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in human resource management (HRM) has reshaped recruitment, performance evaluation, talent mapping, and workforce planning across both private and public sectors. While AI-based systems are widely associated with efficiency, objectivity, and data-driven decision-making, their use in public institutions also raises ethical problems concerning transparency, accountability, fairness, and algorithmic bias. AI systems trained on historical data can reproduce discrimination and reinforce structural inequalities. This article examines ethical AI governance in public HRM by exploring the interaction between human–AI collaboration, algorithmic bias, and institutional accountability. Using a qualitativeconceptual approach grounded in a critical literature review of 41 sources published between 2016 and 2026, complemented by analysis of recent Indonesian regulatory and institutional documents (UU No. 20/2023 on ASN, BKN Circular Letter No. 9/2025, the ASN Digital platform, and the GARUDA AI program), the study finds that Indonesia’s digital bureaucracy faces four structural challenges: a governance gap between AI adoption and regulatory readiness; limited institutional capacity for algorithmic oversight; insufficient AI literacy among HR officials; and the absence of a standardized algorithmic-ethics audit. The article contributes a four-layer ethical-governance model regulatory, institutional, technical, and capability calibrated to Indonesia’s publicadministration context, and argues that AI in public HRM must remain anchored in democratic values, social justice, and human-centred oversight.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools in higher education has raised questions regarding their impact on students’ information literacy (IL) and cognitive processes. In this study, we investigated how generative AI influences undergraduate students’ performance and perceptions in an inorganic chemistry prelaboratory assignment consisting in gathering and elaborating information relevant to the experiments. Second-year chemistry students completed two prelab tasks: one with generative AI support and one without AI. Students reported that generative AI support significantly reduced time dedicated to prelab elaboration. They also perceived AI-assisted tasks as easier and faster, rated AI-generated information as less clear and precise than traditional sources, and frequently expressed concerns about its reliability. However, no statistically significant differences were observed in instructor-evaluated scores between AI-supported and non-AI prelabs. These results indicate that students predominantly valued AI for efficiency. Interpreted through a Cognitive Load Theory lens, the reduction in time and search effort is consistent with a possible decrease in task-related logistical demands.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Human-centered XAI conceptualizes explanations as external representations of model behavior intended to support users’ reasoning and sensemaking, rather than as self-contained artifacts that directly convey understanding. Because their interpretation is shaped by users’ cognitive processes and contextual circumstances, understanding emerges through active engagement in formulating, testing, and refining hypotheses. In exploratory settings, where relevant questions and factors are not fully specified in advance, such engagement relies on iterative questioning, experimentation, and revision, typically mediated through interactive visualization. Hypothetical Scenario (HS)–based XAI methods operationalize this exploratory mode of explanation by enabling users to manipulate input conditions and observe resulting changes in model outputs. Through what-if testing, HS externalizes users’ reasoning processes by instantiating hypotheses as concrete interactions whose consequences become observable. Exploratory interaction, however, is not cognitively neutral. Prior work in cognitive science and human–computer interaction shows that reasoning during exploration is systematically shaped by cognitive biases such as anchoring, availability, and salience. In HS-based exploration, these biases can influence scenario selection, input sampling, outcome comparison, and the sequencing of interactions, leading to incomplete or misleading interpretations even when explanations are technically faithful. Such biases do not manifest as incorrect explanations, but as characteristic interaction behaviors that signal elevated risks of misinterpretation. Accordingly, this paper examines bias-related interpretation risks in HS-based XAI and evaluates whether targeted interface design safeguards can reduce bias-prone interaction patterns. We introduce HypotheX, an interactive HS-based XAI system, and show that interface-level interventions can mitigate some—though not all—such risks.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly entering educational practice, yet its implications for justice and fairness in group work remain underexplored. This exploratory qualitative study examines 28 anonymous written responses collected from a Blended Intensive Programme (BIP) on AI pedagogy and well-being involving higher-education students from five European universities. Participants responded to an open-ended question about how AI affects justice or fairness in education and group work. Using inductive thematic analysis and multi-label coding, the study identified recurring concerns around access, learning support, group-work support, contribution visibility, bias, agency, transparency and assessment. The findings should be read as a pilot mapping of fairness-related perceptions within this specific educational context rather than as representative evidence. We synthesise these perceptions into six preliminary dimensions of AI-mediated collaborative justice: access, contribution, assessment, epistemic and linguistic, agency, and transparency justice. The framework provides a starting point for future research and for the design of fairer AI-supported collaborative learning.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Trust calibration—aligning user trust judgment with model capability—is crucial for safe deployment of explainable AI (XAI), yet is often evaluated via global trust ratings detached from objective performance evidence. We present a preregistered, incentivized between-subject online study (N = 418 representative UK sample) on explainable skin-lesion classification that disentangles expectation-setting from experienced performance. Participants completed 15 case evaluations using a fixed XAI panel (malignancy score, reliability score, and saliency map). We systematically manipulated five experimental onboarding conditions varying example-based information and limitation disclosures with five stimulus packages naturally varying observed prediction quality. Calibration was operationalized as the deviation between trust-related judgments (TAIS and case-wise ratings) and objective performance benchmarks for the encountered cases, analysed with hierarchical mixed-effects models. Only limitation disclosure for case-wise measures reliably impacts trust calibration, and short-term experience did not yield progressive calibration. Further, the experienced package of stimuli explained substantially more variance than the experimental manipulation. However, participants were hard-pressed to differentiate between case-wise perceived trust, trustworthiness, and accuracy estimation. We discuss implications for designing limitation communication and for measuring and analysing calibration metrics in XAI evaluations. All study materials and data of this study are publicly available for replication and further academic use.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has created new opportunities and challenges for instructional practice, prompting universities to explore AI-enabled tools through structured pilot initiatives. This case study examined why faculty in the College of Agricultural and Life Science at the University of Florida chose to participate in a pilot of an AI-supported writing feedback tool and how they experienced its implementation over the course of a semester. A faculty focus group captured their motivations, perceived benefits, challenges, and recommendations for future pilots. The Theory of Planned Behavior and Diffusion of Innovations theory provided a guiding framework for interpreting faculty beliefs, social influences, and perceptions of the tool’s attributes. Findings indicated that faculty were motivated by curiosity, perceived instructional value, and alignment with institutional priorities. Implementation experiences were shaped by tool usability, course fit considerations, student response, and the availability of timely support. Participants emphasized the importance of clear onboarding, transparent communication with students, and opportunities for low‑stakes experimentation. Recommendations included strengthening training, improving integration with existing systems, and establishing ongoing feedback loops between faculty and instructional support units. The study offers practical guidance for designing AI pilot programs and contributes to emerging scholarship‑ on faculty adoption of AI tools in higher education

The increasing availability of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping how students engage with learning and feedback in higher education. While existing research has largely focused on AI-generated feedback and hybrid human–AI feedback approaches, less is known about how students independently use AI to interpret educator feedback. This study investigated how Computer Science students use GenAI tools to understand and act upon educator feedback. Drawing on feedback literacy theory, an exploratory mixed-methods survey was conducted with 140 undergraduate and postgraduate Computer Science students at an Australian university. Overall, 89.0% of respondents reported using AI at least occasionally to interpret educator feedback, primarily to explain unclear comments and suggest improvements. Although students generally perceived AI explanations positively, many also recognised that AI could occasionally misunderstand educator intentions. The study contributes to emerging discussions on AI-mediated feedback literacy by conceptualising generative AI as an intermediary interpretive layer between educator feedback and student action, with implications for feedback design and the development of critical AI literacy in higher education.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Working across disciplines requires educators and students to hold conflicting perspectives in tension, negotiate contested meaning, and integrate knowledge in ways no single discipline allows (Mansilla & Duraising, 2007). Such work is cognitively, emotionally, and socially demanding (Manathunga et al., 2006). Yet this difficulty reflects a well-established finding in education research: that struggle, effort, and a degree of discomfort are not obstacles to learning but conditions for it, provided learners feel safe enough to stay with them (Bjork & Bjork, 2011). As generative AI becomes embedded in higher education, it reshapes not only how knowledge is accessed, but the learning experience itself. This technology holds real value, yet its orientation towards fluent, instantly agreeable output can run counter to this. In practice, it smooths over the uncertainty, disagreement, and difficulty through which interdisciplinary understanding is built, narrowing the epistemic diversity such work depends on (McInnes & Airey, 2025). The question, then, is not whether to use digital tools but when – understanding where they enhance learning, and where they erode this difficulty, is a central design question for technology-enhanced learning. A key challenge for interdisciplinary educators, therefore, is how to design learning that creates space for this discomfort to thrive. While toolkits for interdisciplinary research are now plentiful, resources for teaching it remain scarce (Laursen et al., 2024). Drawing on an extensive review of the literature, we present a seven-stage model for interdisciplinary learning and teaching, spanning reflexivity, teamwork, visioning, wicked problems, disciplinary integration, creative play, and interdisciplinary assessment. The model is grounded in constructive alignment (Biggs, 1996) and draws on transition-based approaches to teaching complex, real-world challenges (Bertolini et al., 2024). Originally designed around a multi-day, face-to-face interactive workshop, the model has since been translated into more practical formats: a board game version, currently being trialled, and a Canvas course in development. Across all formats, the seven stages are not about engineering discomfort but about creating a supportive, structured space in which the tensions intrinsic to interdisciplinary work can be explored directly rather than avoided or bypassed: space for sitting with not-knowing, for productive disagreement, and for the slow work of finding common ground (Colwill & Boyd, 2008). It leans on digital tools where they extend what educators can do, while keeping the work of integration and productive disagreement deliberately analogue. The purpose of this poster is to share the seven-stage model with educators and to sharpen it against the realities of interdisciplinary teaching across different disciplines and institutions. Preparing educators to teach across disciplines, not merely within them, remains an under-served challenge, and this model is a deliberate response to it. In prioritising the relational, embodied, and sometimes uncomfortable work of learning together, it offers a human-centred response to interdisciplinary teaching in an increasingly digital society – where designing for the productive difficulty that interdisciplinary work depends on is not a constraint to be managed but a capacity worth protecting.

Purpose Autonomous delivery robots (ADRs) perform a functional logistics task, yet scenario-based evaluations may depend substantially on whether the robot appears readable and approachable. This study examines how perceived anthropomorphic design cues relate to ADR adoption intention in Hanoi …

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping higher education, yet institutional responses have often prioritised compliance and detection over meaningful student support. While students increasingly engage with GenAI in their learning, responsible use requires more than confidence or technical proficiency. Emerging evidence suggests students want to engage with GenAI responsibly but frequently experience uncertainty, a challenge that is fundamentally one of human-centred learning design rather than academic integrity alone. However, supporting students to become confident GenAI users cannot itself be assumed to be an ethical goal, given the technology’s potential to reproduce bias, exacerbate inequity, compromise privacy and diminish human agency. This paper proposes a human-centred ethical discernment framework grounded in connection, collaboration and compassion. Drawing on insights from qualitative research into undergraduate students’ experiences of GenAI and a practitioner-led redesign at the University of Southern Queensland (UniSQ), the framework integrates storytelling, visual pedagogy and embedded guidance, and structured dialogue to support learner agency and ethical decision making. Informed by care ethics, virtue ethics and justice, the framework positions students as accountable decision-makers capable of using, limiting or rejecting GenAI in response to context, consequence and responsibility. Rather than positioning academic integrity as a compliance exercise, the framework emphasises authentic relationships, learner agency and contextually embedded learning experiences. It offers a relational approach to supporting ethical GenAI engagement while preserving human judgement, accountability and meaningful connection within increasingly digital learning environments.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Monash University has embarked on an ambitious Assessment Advancement project seeing the review of over 500 courses and areas of study redesigned programmatically with intentional integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) to prepare students for an ever-changing world. The Programmatic Assessment and AI Review (PAAIR) project at Monash University is generating rich, expert feedback on course design, assessment regimes, learning outcome alignment, and AI integration across coursework programs (Baartman et al., 2022; Fawns et al., 2026; Heeneman et al., 2021; Sotiriadou et al., 2020). GenAI is intensifying the need for scalable but trustworthy curriculum review practices that preserve human agency, accountability and professional judgement. AI governance guidance emphasises that AI should augment, not displace, human agency, with human oversight, accountability and risk management built into system design (Miao & Holmes, 2023). This poster presents emerging work to use feedback from the PAAIR Panel, a cross-faculty group of Monash education experts, to train an AI agent that can support education teams in reviewing Course Design Spreadsheets as part of course reaccreditation and continuous review. The proposed AI agent is deliberately positioned as an assistant, not a decision-maker. Its role is to highlight areas within a course that may warrant closer human attention, such as unclear alignment between course learning outcomes, unit learning outcomes and assessment tasks; limited evidence of progression across a course; unclear rationale for AI use or restriction; over-reliance on particular assessment types; or places where assessment security may depend too heavily on final products rather than visible evidence of learning. The AI does not replace educational judgement, approve course design, or provide final feedback to course teams. Instead, it prompts reviewers to look more closely, ask better questions, and provide contextualised human feedback. The work responds to a key institutional challenge and a sector-wide response to enacting assessment reform in a time of AI: how to scale educative feedback across large numbers of courses while maintaining the professional judgement, disciplinary sensitivity and care that meaningful course review requires (Lodge et al., 2025). By training the agent on feedback authored by Monash education experts, the project seeks to preserve and amplify local educational expertise rather than outsource it. The AI is being designed to support consistency, reduce reviewer workload, and make recurring patterns visible across submissions, while keeping humans responsible for interpretation, dialogue and decision-making. Achieving these aims without compromising feedback quality is a high priority in our testing. This approach contributes to broader conversations about responsible AI in higher education by exploring a human-in-the-loop model where AI assists educational teams to review complex curriculum data. The AI supports the review while decisions stay with educators. The model could transfer to institutions following a similar review process, though their policy, curriculum templates and staffing will shape feasibility. The poster will share the emerging design principles, potential workflow, and early opportunities for using expert-informed AI to support programmatic assessment and AI integration.

As generative AI reshapes how learners access, generate and engage with knowledge, the tertiary education sector is increasingly developing assessment approaches that better cultivate learner agency, meaningful engagement with feedback, and self-regulated learning. Alongside these developments, longstanding debates about the role of grades have gained renewed prominence, prompting greater attention to how assessment systems support learning, certification, and learner agency. This paper presents an institution-wide exploration of ungraded assessment as one approach to designing assessment that places greater emphasis on dialogue, learner agency, and meaningful feedback. The focus extends beyond evaluating a single assessment model to examine how the University’s central educational practice team, college and school learning and teaching specialists, and academic staff collaboratively explored the relationships between grading, feedback, and learning across different disciplinary contexts. Drawing on practice-informed examples, the paper illustrates how different contexts interpreted and adapted ungraded assessment, from studio-based pedagogies in design to emerging experimentation in computing balancing developmental learning with progression requirements. The paper argues that designing assessment with foregrounds dialogue, learner agency, and meaningful feedback cannot be achieved through assessment task redesign alone; it requires coordinated curriculum, educator capability, and institutional practices. It identifies practice-informed design considerations to strengthen learner agency and sustainable assessment reform in AI-enabled higher education.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how students imagine, produce, revise and communicate creative work. In animation education, AI tools can support rapid ideation, visual experimentation and alternative design pathways, but they also raise questions about how students continue to develop foundational skills, creative judgement, peer critique and reflective practice. This poster presents a classroom-informed visual framework for integrating AI into practice-based creative learning without reducing learning to prompt generation or final outputs. The framework was developed through practice-led curriculum redesign in an undergraduate animation course. It is informed by reflective practice, foundational animation principles, authentic learning, engagement theory and recent debates about AI in higher education (Bearman et al., 2023; Herrington, 2006; Kearsley & Shneiderman, 1998; Schön, 1983; Thomas & Johnston, 1981). Rather than positioning AI as a replacement for craft, critique or student decision-making, the framework maps AI-supported creative learning as an iterative studio process: observe, experiment, generate, critique, reflect, refine and share. This cycle visualises how AI can be embedded within classroom activities while keeping human judgement, feedback, revision and ethical decision-making central to learning. The poster focuses on how this framework can support creative practice in the classroom. It highlights how students may use AI to explore visual possibilities, test ideas, compare alternatives and reflect on their decisions, while still being assessed on process, reasoning, feedback use, authorship and responsible tool engagement. The visual model is organised around four pedagogical commitments: reflection; iteration; collaboration and critique; and ethical decision-making. By foregrounding a practical classroom case and a visual teaching framework, this poster contributes to ASCILITE 2026’s themes of connection, collaboration, creativity and compassion in a digital society. Although grounded in animation education, the model offers transferable strategies for educators designing AI-supported learning in creative, project-based and practice-based courses.

This conceptual paper proposes a conceptual framework for designing Productive Failure-informed AI learning agents that function as pedagogical facilitators rather than answer-providing tools. Grounded in Productive Failure (PF), the framework structures AI-supported learning across three interconnected phases: idea generation and exploration, consolidation, and knowledge assembly. Within each phase, it specifies the role of the AI facilitator, the structure of AI–learner interaction, and the cognitive processes intended to support learning. The framework positions AI agents as mediators that activate prior knowledge, encourage multiple solution attempts, support comparison with canonical knowledge, promote recognition of knowledge gaps, and guide the organisation of emerging understanding into generalisable principles. Theoretically, the framework extends PF into AI-mediated learning contexts by translating its underlying mechanisms into interaction design principles. Practically, it provides educators and developers with a pedagogically grounded approach to designing AI-supported environments that prioritise cognitive engagement, conceptual understanding, and knowledge transfer. Future research should empirically examine the framework across disciplinary, learner, and institutional contexts.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Generative AI raises identity- and values-level questions for higher education staff. Yet professional development in this space remains largely focused on individualised technical and pedagogical skill and capability development, rather than providing structured opportunities for the collective sense-making such questions require. This paper describes the design and delivery of a human-centred workshop developed for a team of higher education third space practitioners to support collective sense-making and values negotiation around AI use. Drawing on reflective practitioner inquiry, we describe the design principles that shaped the workshop and the practical constraints within which it was delivered. We reflect on what worked, including the value of structured formats in supporting deeper engagement, and of workshop artefacts as an evolving record of shared thinking. We suggest this design offers a transferable approach for other educator teams grappling with similar uncertainty, and propose that professional development for AI should complement skills-focused approaches with structured space for the collective exploration of values, judgement, and human agency.

As generative artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into learning environments, its role is shifting from a passive tool to an active partner in meaning-making and creative expression. This study explores how young children engage in co-creative learning with AI through adults and examines the implications of these interactions for reimagining human–AI partnerships in early childhood education. Sixteen children (aged 5-6) from a single preschool classroom first drew an original character and then worked individually alongside a researcher to generate an AI-based version of that character using Gemini, with up to three iterative prompts per child. Data from classroom observations, interaction records, and reflective discussions were analysed using thematic analysis to understand children’s interaction dynamics. Initial findings reveal one key dimension of co-creative engagement. Children appreciated AI’s ability to extend and transform their visual ideas, yet emphasised the importance of maintaining personal authorship and manual control, highlighting an emerging sense of creative agency in human–AI collaboration. Building on these findings, the study proposes a vision of AI as a creative teammate that amplifies children's imagination while preserving human intentionality and ownership.

The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has radically disrupted higher education assessment paradigms (Chung, 2024). Institutional responses to maintaining assessment integrity have primarily focused on defensive mechanisms, such as mitigating risks surrounding written assessments, refining text-matching software, and enforcing restrictive academic integrity policies (Lodge, 2024). However, this reactive posture often overlooks the transformative potential of GenAI as a student’s and lecturer’s long-term coach in authentic assessment design (Atif, 2024). This research-in-progress pivots away from deficit-based AI detection, proposing instead the integration of VirtualSpeech GenAI avatars to converse with students during a recorded viva, generating verifiable, real-time student output. By replacing static written tasks with dynamic oral assessments, this relatively new form of creative expression maintains authentic student contributions to improve AI literacy, strengthen authorship verification, eliminate academic outsourcing, and simultaneously cultivate sophisticated negotiation skills (Perkins, 2026). This study represents an exemplary innovation of practice by reframing AI not as an academic threat, but as a dual-mode learning and assessment avatar. Rather than engaging with AI purely for text generation, students interact with GenAI avatars (such as VirtualSpeech) simulating realistic corporate stakeholders. This work is strongly anchored in the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, which guides the deliberate alignment of GenAI technology, modern pedagogy, and discipline-specific knowledge (Mishra & Koehler, 2006). This framework assists educators in leveraging immersive technology to redefine pedagogical delivery, facilitating AI literacy and negotiation skills. This research addresses a critical gap in current Technology Enhanced Learning (TEL) literature by investigating the following central question: How are students’ AI literacy and negotiation skills developed when conversing with GenAI avatars as part of a viva presentation? Adopting a design-based research methodology, this project emphasizes the iterative refinement of an educational intervention within an authentic setting (Hoadley & Campos, 2022; Scott et al., 2020). The study is currently in its first implementation cycle within a major tertiary institution, featuring a sample size of 150 second-year Project Management students. Participants are required to defend a project proposal during a live, assessable viva presentation conducted with a customized VirtualSpeech avatar trained to act as a client. This oral format diminishes the appeal of cognitive offloading because students must defend their reasoning under unseen, real-time questioning (Sotiriadou et al., 2020; Tan, 2026). Data collection relies on a mixed-methods approach, utilizing pre- and post-intervention surveys alongside qualitative analysis of student reflections. Preliminary quantitative results indicate a statistically significant increase in both self-reported IT literacy, validating the avatar’s efficacy as a formative and summative tool. This research significantly advances TEL research and practice by providing a protocol for proactive AI integration. While piloted within a project management curriculum, broad applicability across tertiary contexts exists (Cela-Ranilla, 2025). Any discipline requiring high-stakes communication, critical thinking, and stakeholder management—such as business, law, or education—can adapt this viva model. Ultimately, this work demonstrates how universities can safeguard academic integrity not by restricting technology, but leveraging it to create robust, future-focused verbal assessments, requiring students to perform and defend understanding live.

Purpose This study examines how employee-perceived generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) governance maturity relates to approved enterprise use and unauthorized public-tool use in data-sensitive work.
