documents.abstract: Universities govern AI adoption through artefacts. Policies, rubrics, assessment briefs, vendor evaluation frameworks, and design templates cross organisational boundaries and carry meaning differently in each context. This paper applies the concept of boundary objects within a cultural-historical activity theory (CHAT) framework to analyse which artefacts effectively mediate AI governance across academic, institutional, and commercial activity systems, and which fail. Drawing on the author’s framework for negotiated legitimacy in interacting activity systems and reflexive practitioner experience as an education design leader, the paper develops a typology of AI governance boundary objects classified by origin, interpretive flexibility, and failure mode. The analysis identifies three structural conditions that determine whether a boundary object supports or undermines the legitimacy of learning designers who broker AI adoption across systems. These are co-design across activity systems, support for transformation rather than coordination alone, and resistance to capture by a single system’s logic. It also identifies a failure dynamic specific to generative AI, in which an unstable referent causes artefacts to decay. The paper offers practical design principles for governance artefacts and connects them to a wider question, namely how institutions keep human and pedagogical judgement central as they adopt digital technologies.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in higher education, yet much of its use positions AI as a private productivity tool for generating answers, feedback or text. This paper argues that AI is not educational simply because it produces outputs. From a sociocultural perspective, its educational significance emerges when pedagogical design transforms it from an artefact into a mediating tool for participation in disciplinary learning. The paper introduces the AI Mediated Participation Framework, grounded in mediated learning, appropriation and participation. It proposes three design principles: preserving learner ownership, scaffolding thinking through dialogue, and developing AI literacy through disciplinary practice. These principles operate through questioning, dialogue, reflection, critical evaluation and decision making to support learner agency, evaluative judgement, responsible AI use, critical thinking and knowledge construction. The framework is illustrated through AI learning activities in undergraduate and postgraduate educational research courses, where educator modelling, peer discussion and disciplinary expectations repositioned AI from a private feedback service to a mediating tool for methodological reasoning and researcher judgement. The framework shifts attention from what AI can do to how pedagogical design determines what AI becomes educationally.

As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in the workplace, limited research has examined how job demands shape employees' behavioral and motivational responses in human-AI collaboration and how resources influence these relationships. Drawing on Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) theory, this study adopts a mixed-methods approach, combining semi-structured interviews with 15 participants (10 employees and 5 graduate students) to explore relevant job demands and resources, followed by a cross-sectional survey yielding 282 valid responses to test the research model. The findings show that job demand is positively associated with cyberloafing and negatively associated with job engagement. Anthropomorphism strengthens the positive association between job demand and cyberloafing while weakening its negative association with job engagement. Cognitive support also strengthens the former relationship but does not significantly moderate the latter. These findings extend JD-R theory to human-AI collaboration by highlighting the differentiated roles of resources across behavioral and motivational outcomes. They also suggest that anthropomorphic AI may help sustain job engagement under demanding conditions, while its association with cyberloafing warrants careful consideration.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly entering knowledge work, and its short-term productivity benefits are increasingly documented. Less is known about what happens, over time, to the knowledge, skills, and judgment that remain in people and organizations. This integrative narrative review addresses that question through the construct of cognitive capital: the accumulated, renewable, and depletable stock of knowledge, cognitive, and metacognitive capabilities, and practices that enable an individual or an organization to learn, interpret information, exercise judgment, solve problems, and adapt. We distinguish individual and organizational cognitive capital from the capability of the human-AI system, so that gains in joint performance and losses in human capability can be observed at the same time. Drawing on experimental, field, and conceptual work, we propose four mechanisms through which interaction with AI affects cognitive capital: substitution of practice, scaffolding and feedback, metacognitive calibration, and organizational aggregation. Seven principles summarize the current evidence, including that assisted performance differs from retained competence, that the same technology can support or displace learning depending on design and use, and that individual gains can coexist with reduced collective diversity. For each mechanism, we derive testable propositions, and we discuss five design levers for organizations as proposals to be validated rather than established practice. We conclude that cognitive capital offers a multilevel frame for governing AI adoption and outline a research agenda centered on longitudinal, multilevel measurement.

Educators are increasingly turning to generative AI when developing teaching materials, yet most research to date has centred on student-facing applications. This paper presents a work-in-progress study that asks a different question: what happens to an educator’s design judgment when AI enters the case-writing process? Two business educators – one in accounting, one in management – will each develop a teaching case study using AI-assisted workflows, documenting their prompts, editorial decisions, and reasoning through structured process logs. Drawing on Schön’s (1983) reflective practitioner framework and Abell’s (1997) 10 criteria for effective teaching cases, the study examines where human expertise proves essential and where AI contributes meaningfully. The pairing of two sub-disciplines, management accounting and management, allows us to examine whether disciplinary knowledge shapes these design decisions in distinct ways, although the study’s central concern remain the design judgement itself. Early observations from the instrument development phase point to a useful distinction: AI appears better suited to qualities that require evaluative judgment (structure, data accuracy, length) than those demanding generative judgment (ambiguity, controversy, authentic voice). We expect further patterns to emerge once data collection begins. This paper outlines the research design and its anticipated contributions.

This non-empirical conceptual analysis examines how artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming woven into curriculum production, assessment, feedback, student support, academic integrity, accessibility and institutional decision-making. These systems are often justified through connection: faster feedback, personalised support, scalable services and more efficient learning design. Yet technical connection is not the same as educational connection. AI may leave the visible forms of university learning intact while weakening academic authorship, assessment validity, student trust, staff agency, care, equity and institutional legitimacy. The paper develops refusal-capable design: the distributed institutional capacity to decide when AI should be adopted, constrained, redesigned or refused. It integrates connected learning, responsible innovation, sociotechnical studies of educational technology, care ethics, justice-oriented educational judgment and technology non-use scholarship, using selected public examples illustratively rather than as an empirical sample. Six heuristic refusal zones organise recurring legitimacy tensions, and the Distributed Refusal-Capable University Design Cycle translates those tensions into accountable redesign. The contribution is a practical and theoretical account of refusal as a legitimate design outcome rather than simple opposition to AI.
